title: Modes and Stability
intro: Some starting states give a motion that is nothing but a single exponential along a straight line: these are the modes, and they are the eigenvectors of $A$. Every other motion is a sum of modes, so the eigenvalues tell you whether the system returns to rest, how fast, and what shape the path takes in the state plane.

blocks.text: A start that stays on a line

Look for a starting state $v$ whose free motion keeps pointing the same way: $x(t) = f(t)\,v$ for some scalar function $f$. Put it into $x' = Ax$: the left side is $f'(t)v$ and the right side is $f(t)Av$. They can only agree if $Av$ is a multiple of $v$, say $Av = \lambda v$, and then $f' = \lambda f$, so $f = e^{\lambda t}$. That is the definition of an eigenvector, and the result is the statement of this section:

blocks.tex: x(0) = v,\quad Av = \lambda v \quad\Rightarrow\quad x(t) = e^{\lambda t}\,v

blocks.text: A motion of this form is a mode. It stays on the line through $v$ for ever; it moves along that line towards the origin if $\lambda < 0$, away from it if $\lambda > 0$, and does not move if $\lambda = 0$. You can see the same fact from $e^{At}v = e^{\lambda t}v$, since every power $A^kv = \lambda^kv$ in the series. The eigenvalues and eigenvectors themselves are found on the Eigenvalues pages, and the viewer draws the eigen-lines as dashed lines.
A general start is a mix of modes
A system with two independent eigenvectors $v_1, v_2$ can be started anywhere, because any $x(0)$ can be written as $c_1v_1 + c_2v_2$. By linearity each part runs its own mode:

blocks.tex: x(0) = c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x(t) = c_1e^{\lambda_1t}v_1 + c_2e^{\lambda_2t}v_2

blocks.text: Take the heavily damped mass, $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{pmatrix}$, with $\lambda_1 = -1$ along $v_1 = (1, -1)$ and $\lambda_2 = -2$ along $v_2 = (1, -2)$ (found on the page Solving the State Equations (#/math/state-space/solving)). Released from $x(0) = (1, 0)$, the mass is pulled aside by 1 m and let go. To find $c_1$ and $c_2$ write the equation $c_1(1, -1) + c_2(1, -2) = (1, 0)$ as two equations, $c_1 + c_2 = 1$ and $-c_1 - 2c_2 = 0$. The second gives $c_1 = -2c_2$; the first then gives $-c_2 = 1$, so $c_2 = -1$ and $c_1 = 2$. Therefore

This agrees with the first column of $e^{At}$ computed on the previous page. At $t = 1$ the two parts are $(0.736, -0.736)$ and $(-0.135, 0.271)$, adding to $x(1) = (0.600, -0.465)$. The fast mode ($e^{-2t}$) dies out first, and from then on the state is nearly $2e^{-t}(1, -1)$: the path bends onto the slow eigen-line and slides down it. At $t = 4$ the fast part is about $0.0003$ while the slow one is $0.037$, so the state is $(0.036, -0.036)$ to three places.

blocks.text: The System is the heavily damped mass, Input none. The dashed eigen-lines are blue for the pole with the larger $|\lambda|$ ($-2$) and teal for the other ($-1$). Start with $x_1(0) = 1$, $x_2(0) = 0$: the dark path leaves the point $(1, 0)$, heads straight down at first (the arrow there is $(0, -2)$), and bends onto the teal line, which is the slow mode. Now set $x_2(0)$ to $-1$: the start is on the teal line itself, and the path is a straight line into the origin. Try $x_2(0) = -2$ with $x_1(0) = 1$, which is on the blue line: another straight path, faster. Step 4 of the walk-through (Next step ▶) moves $x(0)$ onto the slow line, $(1.0, -1.0)$, for you.
Complex modes: decaying rotations

When $\lambda = \sigma + j\omega$ is complex, the eigenvector is complex too, and so is $e^{\lambda t}v$. But the system is real, so the real part and the imaginary part of that solution are each a real solution. For the RLC circuit, $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\lambda = -1 + j$, solve $(A - \lambda I)v = 0$: the first row is $(1 - j)v_1 + 2v_2 = 0$, so $v = (2,\ -1 + j)$. Check with the second row, $-v_1 + (-2 - \lambda)v_2 = -2 + (-1 - j)(-1 + j) = -2 + 2 = 0$, since $(-1-j)(-1+j) = 1 - j^2 = 2$. Now expand $e^{(-1+j)t}v$ with $e^{jt} = \cos t + j\sin t$:

blocks.tex: e^{-t}(\cos t + j\sin t)\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 + j \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathrm{Re}: \ e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix} 2\cos t \\ -\cos t - \sin t \end{pmatrix}

blocks.text: The real part is the motion that starts at $\mathrm{Re}\,v = (2, -1)$. It turns round the origin once every $2\pi/\omega = 6.28$ s while its size shrinks by $e^{-t}$: a decaying rotation, a spiral. The two numbers read off at once: the real part $\sigma = -1$ is the decay rate, and the imaginary part $\omega = 1$ is the turning rate. See Complex Eigenvalues and Rotation (#/math/eigenvalues/complex-eigenvalues) for rotation with complex eigenvalues.

When does the system return to rest?
Every free motion is a sum of terms $e^{\lambda_it}$ (times $t$, if eigenvalues repeat), so everything depends on the real parts. The definitions:

items: Asymptotically stable: every motion tends to $0$. This holds exactly when every eigenvalue has $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda < 0$.

Unstable: some motion grows without bound. This happens as soon as one eigenvalue has $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda > 0$ (and also when an eigenvalue on the imaginary axis is repeated and defective, because the factor $t$ then makes the term grow: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ gives $x = (x_1(0) + t\,x_2(0),\ x_2(0))$).

Marginally stable: no motion grows, but some do not decay either. All $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda \le 0$, and the eigenvalues with $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda = 0$ are not defective: each has as many independent eigenvectors as its multiplicity, which is automatic when it is simple, so no factor $t$ appears. An undamped oscillator is the standard example: a mass on a spring with no friction swings for ever.

blocks.text: Going through the presets, using the poles the viewer prints:

items: Light mass, poles $-0.5 \pm 1.936j$: stable (spiral in). Heavy mass, $-1$ and $-2$: stable (no oscillation). RLC circuit, $-1 \pm j$: stable. Two tanks, $-1$ and $-0.5$: stable.
Undamped oscillator, $\pm j$: marginal. The state goes round a closed loop and never settles. Negative damping, $0.15 \pm 0.989j$: unstable, a spiral that grows by $e^{0.15t}$.

Pendulum balanced upright, $+1$ and $-1$: unstable. DC motor, $0$ and $-2$: the viewer says 'on the edge'. The state does not blow up by itself (free, the speed dies away and the angle stops at a constant), but a constant input drives the angle without limit, as the previous page showed. Marginal stability is a fragile property.

blocks.text: A different kind of stability, bounded-input bounded-output, asks whether bounded inputs give bounded outputs. For these systems it also needs every pole of the transfer function in the left half-plane, but a pole can hide from the output, as the page Transfer Functions and Realisations (#/math/state-space/transfer-functions) shows.
The test for two states: trace and determinant

For $A$ of size $2 \times 2$ the eigenvalues satisfy $\lambda^2 - \tau\lambda + \Delta = 0$, where $\tau = \mathrm{tr}\,A$ and $\Delta = \det A$. (They follow from $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \tau$ and $\lambda_1\lambda_2 = \Delta$.) Then, with no need to find the roots:

items: If the roots are real, $\Delta = \lambda_1\lambda_2 > 0$ means the same sign, and $\tau = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 < 0$ means that sign is negative. If $\Delta < 0$ the signs differ: one root is positive.
If the roots are complex, they are $\tau/2 \pm j\omega$, so their real part is $\tau/2$, negative exactly when $\tau < 0$; and $\Delta = (\tau/2)^2 + \omega^2$ is automatically positive.

blocks.text: So the 2×2 system is asymptotically stable if and only if $\tau < 0$ and $\Delta > 0$. Check: light mass $\tau = -1$, $\Delta = 4$, stable. Heavy mass, $\tau = -3$, $\Delta = 2$, stable. RLC, $\tau = -2$, $\Delta = 2$. Two tanks, $\tau = -1.5$, $\Delta = 0.5$. Pendulum, $\tau = 0$, $\Delta = -1$: unstable. Negative damping, $\tau = 0.3 > 0$: unstable. Undamped, $\tau = 0$, $\Delta = 1$: the borderline. The discriminant $\tau^2 - 4\Delta$ decides real against complex: it is $1 - 16 = -15$ for the light mass (complex) and $9 - 8 = 1$ for the heavy one (real).
Speed: time constants and the slowest pole

A real pole $\lambda < 0$ has a time constant $1/|\lambda|$, the time in which that mode shrinks by a factor $e$. For a complex pair the decay is set by the real part: $1/|\sigma|$. After four time constants a mode has shrunk to $e^{-4} \approx 1.8\%$. The slowest mode, the pole closest to the imaginary axis, decides the settling time, about $4/|\sigma|$. For the heavy mass that is $4/1 = 4$ s, and indeed the free motion from $(1, 0)$ is down to $0.036$ at $t = 4$ s. For the light mass, $\sigma = -0.5$, so the oscillation takes about $8$ s to die; the viewer's plot runs to $10$ s for it, five time constants of the slowest mode. The fast mode of the heavy mass, time constant $0.5$ s, is long gone by then and does not matter. This is why the slowest poles are called dominant.
The shapes in the state plane

The pictures of $2 \times 2$ systems have names. If both eigenvalues are real and of the same sign, the paths run along the eigen-lines into (or out of) the origin: a node (the heavy mass above). If the real eigenvalues have opposite signs, the paths come in along the stable line and leave along the unstable line, a saddle (the pendulum). If the eigenvalues are complex with a non-zero real part, the paths spiral (the light mass, the RLC circuit; or outwards for negative damping). If they are purely imaginary, the paths are closed loops around the origin: a centre (the undamped oscillator). In terms of $\tau$ and $\Delta$: $\Delta < 0$ is a saddle; $\Delta > 0$ with $\tau^2 > 4\Delta$ is a node; $\Delta > 0$ with $\tau^2 < 4\Delta$ is a spiral if $\tau \ne 0$ and a centre if $\tau = 0$. These shapes, and what becomes of them for nonlinear systems, are the subject of the next topic in the Math list, Phase-Space Dynamics, which is planned and not yet written.
The pendulum's saddle

The upright pendulum, $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, has $\lambda = +1$ along $(1, 1)$ and $\lambda = -1$ along $(1, -1)$. Start exactly on the stable line, $x(0) = (1, -1)$: the motion is $e^{-t}(1, -1)$ and the pendulum drifts calmly to the upright position. It is a knife edge, since the tiniest component along $(1, 1)$ grows like $e^{t}$. Split $x(0) = (1, -0.9)$ into $a(1,1) + b(1,-1)$: $a + b = 1$ and $a - b = -0.9$ give $a = 0.05$ and $b = 0.95$. At $t = \ln 30 \approx 3.4$ s the growing part is $0.05 \times 30 = 1.5$ in each state and the stable part has shrunk to $0.95/30 = 0.03$: $x(3.4) = (1.53, 1.47)$.

blocks.text: The System is the pendulum balanced upright, Input none, $x_1(0) = 1$, $x_2(0) = -0.9$: a start close to the dashed line labelled $\lambda = -1$ but not on it. The path first heads down the line towards the origin, then turns, and runs out along the line $\lambda = 1$. The readout ends 'At t = 3.4 s: x = (1.53, 1.47)', which matches the sum above. Now set $x_2(0) = -1.0$ exactly: the path is a straight line into the origin and the readout ends 'x = (0.03, −0.03)'. Honestly, that is what the picture shows. The viewer computes in floating point, so its start carries a rounding error of about $10^{-16}$ along the unstable line, but the plot stops at 3.4 s, and in that time the error grows only 30-fold: far too small to see, so the path stays on the line. An error of $10^{-16}$ would reach size 1 only after $\ln 10^{16} \approx 37$ s, which is far beyond the plot; a real pendulum, with disturbances much bigger than $10^{-16}$, peels off far sooner. Step 4 of the walk-through starts you on that stable line; if you press Play ▶ and keep your eye on the end of the path you see it decay.
Lyapunov: stability without eigenvalues

There is a second way to test stability that does not need the eigenvalues, and that carries over to nonlinear systems. Look for a bowl-shaped function $V(x) = x^{\top}Px$ with $P$ symmetric and positive definite, which the motion must always go downhill on. Along a solution $V' = (x')^{\top}Px + x^{\top}Px' = x^{\top}(A^{\top}P + PA)x$. If you can find $P$ such that

blocks.tex: A^{\top}P + PA = -Q \quad\text{with } Q \text{ positive definite (for instance } Q = I\text{)}

blocks.text: then $V' = -x^{\top}Qx < 0$: the bowl is always going down, so the state must go to $0$. The theorem: $A$ is asymptotically stable if and only if for some (equivalently every) positive definite $Q$ this Lyapunov equation has a positive definite solution $P$. For the heavy mass with $Q = I$ write $P = \begin{pmatrix} p_1 & p_2 \\ p_2 & p_3 \end{pmatrix}$. Then $PA$ has rows $(-2p_2,\ p_1 - 3p_2)$ and $(-2p_3,\ p_2 - 3p_3)$, and $A^{\top}P + PA = PA + (PA)^{\top}$ gives three equations:
So $P = \begin{pmatrix} 5/4 & 1/4 \\ 1/4 & 1/4 \end{pmatrix}$. It is positive definite: $p_1 > 0$ and $\det P = 5/16 - 1/16 = 1/4 > 0$. Stability is confirmed without ever finding $-1$ and $-2$.
Practice

blocks.title: Classify by trace and determinant
blocks.text: Without finding eigenvalues, decide the type of $A = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ and of $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
solution: First matrix: $\tau = -2$, $\Delta = (-1)(-1) - (2)(-3) = 1 + 6 = 7$. Since $\tau < 0$ and $\Delta > 0$ it is stable. The discriminant is $\tau^2 - 4\Delta = 4 - 28 = -24 < 0$, so the eigenvalues are complex: a stable spiral. (They are $-1 \pm j\sqrt 6$.)
Second matrix: $\tau = 1$, $\Delta = 0 - 6 = -6 < 0$: a saddle, unstable. The roots are real, of opposite signs: $\lambda^2 - \lambda - 6 = (\lambda - 3)(\lambda + 2)$.
blocks.answer: First: stable spiral. Second: saddle, eigenvalues $3$ and $-2$.

blocks.title: Split a start into modes
blocks.text: For the two tanks, $A = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$ has $\lambda = -1$ along $(1, -2)$ and $\lambda = -0.5$ along $(0, 1)$. Write $x(0) = (1, 0)$ as a mix of the modes and give $x(2)$.
solution: Solve $c_1(1, -2) + c_2(0, 1) = (1, 0)$: the first entry gives $c_1 = 1$; the second gives $-2 + c_2 = 0$, so $c_2 = 2$.

blocks.title: How long to settle
blocks.text: The light mass has poles $-0.5 \pm 1.936j$. How many seconds until the envelope $e^{-0.5t}$ is below $1\%$ of its start? How many oscillations is that?
solution: The period is $2\pi/\omega = 6.283/1.936 = 3.245$ s, so $9.21/3.245 = 2.84$ oscillations.

blocks.title: A Lyapunov check
blocks.text: Is $P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ a Lyapunov matrix for $A = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$? For $Q = I$ does the equation $A^{\top}P + PA = -Q$ hold?
solution: With $P = I$, $A^{\top}P + PA = A^{\top} + A = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 3 \\ 3 & -4 \end{pmatrix}$. It is not $-I$, so $P = I$ does not solve the equation with $Q = I$.

But the theorem asks only that $-(A^{\top}P + PA)$ be positive definite. Here $-(A^{\top} + A) = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $8 - 9 = -1 < 0$, so it is not positive definite. So $V = x_1^2 + x_2^2$ is not a Lyapunov function for this $A$, even though $A$ is stable (eigenvalues $-1$ and $-2$): the distance from the origin can grow for a while, and a different $P$ is needed.
blocks.answer: No: $-(A^{\top} + A)$ has determinant $-1$. The system is stable; this $P$ just does not prove it.
